## Executive Summary
An e-commerce company built a new landing page to increase conversions and ran an A/B test on 294,478 users. This project answers the real business question: ship it, keep the current page, or test longer. With the full statistical rigor. This project covers data contamination handling, a sample-ratio-mismatch check, a confidence interval, and a power analysis distinguishing "no effect" from "not enough data."
:::

## The Verdict

**Do not ship the new page.** The difference in conversion rate is not statistically significant (p = 0.905), and the 95% confidence interval for the difference spans zero. A power analysis confirms this null result is trustworthy. The test can reliably detect an effect as small as 0.35 percentage points, and the observed effect falls within the range it could not distinguish from noise.

| Metric | Control (Old Page) | Treatment (New Page) |
|:---|:---:|:---:|
| Conversion Rate | 12.039% | 11.881% |
| Sample Size | 145,274 | 145,310 |

## Methodology

1. **Data cleaning**: 1.32% of rows had a mismatched group/page assignment (e.g. a "control" user who saw the new page) and were excluded, since their behavior can't be attributed to either version. Duplicate user IDs were also removed, keeping the first occurrence.
2. **Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) check**: verified the ~50/50 split was healthy (chi-square p=0.947) before trusting any downstream comparison.
3. **Main test**: one-sided two-proportion z-test (H1: new page conversion > old page conversion), with a 95% confidence interval for the absolute difference.
4. **Power analysis**: calculated the minimum detectable effect at 80% power given the actual sample size, to distinguish a genuine null result from an underpowered one.
5. **Daily trend check**: examined conversion rate by day across the 23-day test window to rule out a novelty effect.

## Why This Project

Traditional A/B testing portfolio projects stop at "the p-value was above/below 0.05." This one demonstrates the parts that separate a rigorous analyst from a p-value lookup. Catching real data contamination before trusting a result, verifyies randomization health via an SRM check, and correctly interpreting a null result by checking whether the test was even powered to detect a meaningful effect in the first place.
